Introduction

This chapter describes criteria for evaluating permanent impairment of the cardiovascular system and their effects on the individual’s abil-ity to perform activities of daily living (ADLs). The chapter has changed from the previous edi-tion, reflecting a combined approach to all aspects of the cardiovascular system. For the purpose of this impairment rating scheme the cardiovascular system will be divided into the following compo-nents: Valvular Heart Disease, Coronary Artery Disease, Cardiomyopathies, Pericardial Disease, Dysrhythmias, Hypertensive Cardiovascular Disease, Peripheral Vascular Disease (both upper and lower extremities), and Diseases of the Pulmonary Artery.

This chapter provides a brief overview of principles of cardiovascular assessment. The most recently published guidelines from the American Heart Association and the American College of Cardiology are the primary references used in this chapter. The reader is also encouraged to review other publica-tions from the American Medical Association.1 Additionally, a brief discussion will be provided on the use of contemporary diagnostic testing,

including the use of specific laboratory data such as B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) and use of myocar-dial imaging.

4.1 Principles of Assessment

Substantial transformation is apparent throughout this edition of the AMA Guides. The reader must read Chapters 1 and 2 in their entirety and must understand the key concepts and philosophy of the Guides before attempting to use this chapter. The functional impairment classes have been standard-ized, and each cardiovascular disease entity will include its own functional impairment table, main-taining a standard format. A new concept, “Burden of Treatment,” has been introduced in the Sixth Edition and relates well to impairment ratings from cardiovascular disease. As the data shows, the inci-dence of death due to coronary artery disease (CAD) is declining; however, secondary to the survival suc-cess, the incidence of heart failure (HF) continues to increase. Please note that heart failure is the recom-mended term, as there are many causes of HF, not all of which are congestive. Most disease survivors are therefore receiving treatment and lead productive lives, but absent treatment they would have limited function, leading to greater impairment.

4.1a Exercise Testing

Functional capacity is objectively determined and should be used for impairment ratings. There are several standard exercise protocols, which estimate energy expenditure (METs). Table 4-2 outlines the usual treadmill protocols. Although METs may be estimated from treadmill testing, it is preferable to measure energy expenditure using a metabolic sys-tem that employs protocols such as bicycle ergome-try (Table 4-3). In addition to functional capacity based on exercise protocols, most stress testing is combined with myocardial imaging. Myocardial perfusion imaging uses nuclear isotopes to evaluate perfusion defects in the myocardium, representing previous infarction or current myocardial ischemia. Myocardial perfusion imaging when used with stress testing provides additional evidence for the degree of myocardial damage or ischemia.3,4 Stress echocar-diography is also an objective measure that could be used as an alternative.2-4 Stress testing is preferably accomplished by exercise, but when needed, phar-macologic-induced testing can be employed.

4.1b Left Ventricular Function Evaluation

Left ventricular function is an important component in assessing impairment in an individual with virtu-ally any form of cardiac assessment. It is equally important to recognize that both systolic and dia-stolic dysfunction can lead to HF. Both systolic and diastolic dysfunction may be measured and quanti-fied by standard echocardiography.5

Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), a mea-sure of systolic function, is the percentage of blood contained in the ventricle at end diastole that is ejected in systole. Ejection fraction (EF) may be measured by echocardiography, radionuclide angi-ography (multiple gated acquisition, or MUGA), left ventriculography during diagnostic left-sided heart catheterization, computed tomography (CT), and car-diac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). An EF is considered normal if it is greater than 50%. Ejection fraction values can be described as mild dysfunc-tion of 41% to 50%, moderate dysfunction of 30% to 40%, and severe dysfunction of less than 30%.

Both diastolic and systolic dysfunction can result in significant difficulties, which may range from mild dyspnea to pulmonary edema. Quantifying the degree of diastolic dysfunction can be problematic; however, it is manifest clinically as symptoms of HF in the face of normal systolic function and no signifi-cant valvular disease. A recent laboratory test has been developed that is useful for determining the presence or absence of HF. B-type natriuretic peptide or the closely related N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) is released when ventricular wall tension is increased. Clinically, the value is used to deter-mine whether shortness of breath is, in fact, due to actual congestive HF (CHF) or to other processes.8-10 Assays for BNP vary for each laboratory. The BNP also varies by age, sex, and body size. The degree of elevation needs to be assessed in the context of the normal values for each particular laboratory. The BNP level is now included in the impairment tables as an objective measure of active HF.

Methodology for Determining the Grade in an Impairment Class

This chapter employs impairment grids for use in determining the appropriate impairment class (class) and severity grade (grade) in a class for the condi-tion or conditions being rated at Maximum Medical Improvement (MMI). As was stated in Chapter 1, the decision regarding which key factor is the primary determinant of impairment will be clearly stated for each organ system impairment grid selected. The examiner will use this key factor to determine the appropriate class. Once the class has been deter-mined, based on this key factor, the final impairment grade in that class must then be determined by non-key factors, and it is not possible to move upward or downward between classes based on these non-key factors. For most impairment rating scenarios, the middle grade (integer) in a class will serve as the initial (default) rating (Table 4-4).

In many situations, the examiner will then use the non-key factors to determine the grade as being

either a higher or lower severity than the default. For each impairment rating grid in this chapter, classes 1 through 4 will include 5 potential grades.

In order to consistently determine the appropriate impairment grade for a given class, the following procedure is recommended:

1. Determine the impairment class (IC) first, according to the “key factor” for that particular impairment grid.

2. Default to the middle (“C”) grade position for that IC.

3. For the first remaining (non-key) factor, deter-mine the most appropriate IC position and record the number difference to the key factor IC.

4. Repeat step 3 for each remaining (non-key) factor.

5. Summate the IC column differences and add or subtract the final number from the default identi-fied in step 1 to determine the final impairment grade.

To illustrate, if the key factor identifies IC 3 (default to 3C), and non-key factors identify IC 1 and 4, this would produce differences of −2 and +1, respectively. These summate to −1. Subtracting 1 grade from IC/grade 3C gives a final IC/grade of 3B.

In this example, if the non-key factors both identi-fied IC 1, you would summate the diffrerences to −4. Since this procedure does not allow jumping from one IC to a lower (or higher) IC, you would subtract the maximum allowable 2 grades, for a final IC/grade of 3A.

If the key factor indicated class 4C, and both non-key factors were also IC 4, the differences would summate to zero, and IC/grade 4D or 4E would not be possible. In order to correct this deficiency, if the

The process of assigning impairment according to the generic template is as follows:

1. The examiner should note that throughout this chapter the objective test results are used as the primary, or key factor in the impairment rating for the condition, as well-validated functional test measures exist for the cardiovascular system. Using the key impairment factor (objective test results), the patient is assigned an impairment class, with the median as the default position.

2. Each impairment class has a corresponding range of available impairment grades. The examiner should consider the range in each class as divis-ible into 5 subsections. The first is the lowest impairment rating that could be assigned for the class; the fifth is the highest.

3. The NYHA class is the primary basis for his-tory. For the sake of simplicity and consistency, the authors have elected to use the NYHA classification throughout the various tables. However, it must be recognized that there are other validated functional instruments for car-diovascular disorders, such as the Canadian Cardiovascular Society classification system for angina pectoris,2 Seattle Angina Questionnaire,11 and the Minnesota Living With Heart Failure Questionnaire.12 If examiners opt to use any other assessment tool, they must justify their decision explicitly.

4. When secondary factors such as history, physi-cal exam, or ADLs are reviewed, they move the impairment rating up or down within the same class only if they are from a different class. The grade level may be moved to reflect the impact of each secondary factor. The impairment rating will never move out of the class to which it was initially assigned by the objective key factor.

For example, a patient has an echocardiogram that places his or her heart disease in class 2. The default, median (midposition) value is 17%. The range of impairment grades is 11% to 23%, with this range being defined by the specific integers of 11, 14, 17, 20, 23. The patient in our hypothetical example has a NYHA class of II. This is in the same class

as the objective factor, so there is no change in the rating. The physical examination shows no mini-mal changes, consistent with a class 1 examination. This examination, being from a lower class than the original objective test, moves the impairment rating down 1 grade, in this case to 14%. The final impair-ment rating will come from 1 of these 5 integers (they are not an open range of numbers), but the examiner must specifically identify 1 impairment number.

4.2 Valvular Heart Disease

4.2a Criteria for Rating Impairment due to Valvular Heart Disease

Causes of valvular heart disease include calcific or age-related changes, congenital disease, rheumatic disease, and infectious endocarditis. Trauma is rarely a factor. Valvular heart disease may be asymptom-atic or may produce signs or symptoms of CHF or dysrhythmia. Left or right ventricular hypertrophy, ventricular dilation, or ventricular dysfunction may occur.

Doppler echocardiography is a noninvasive, effective tool for evaluation of valvular heart disease. Doppler echocardiography estimates valvular gradients to quantify severity of stenosis,5,13 enables cardiac chamber measurements, and can also help quantify regurgitation. However, the degree of regurgitation is also dependent on the hemodynamic status of the individual, which may vary sequentially between 2 studies.14 Standard echocardiography and degree of dilation, which are crucial to the evaluation of severity, can be applied to the functional impairment Table 4-5 to formulate an impairment estimate.

Diagnostic left-sided heart catheterization is usually not necessary to evaluate patients with either stenotic or regurgitant valvular heart disease. The main indi-cations for such evaluation would be discrepancies between the clinical presentation or examination and the echocardiographic assessment, if the echocardio-graphic assessment were technically deficient, or for planned surgical intervention.

Valvular replacement is common for advanced valvular heart disease. Valvular repair is also cur-rently a proven option for many patients and has become the procedure of choice for most patients with isolated mitral valve insufficiency. Valvular operations may result in class 1 or class 2 degrees of impairment.

Valvular heart disease resulting in HF typically requires dietary modifications and medications to minimize symptoms. Such modifications are included in the impairment classification table (Table 4-5).

CLASS 0 0% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 4-1: VALVULAR HEART DISEASE

Subject: 22-year-old woman.

History: Asymptomatic, echocardiogram done as part of a health fair.

Current Symptoms: None. No signs of cardiac enlargement, HF, or cardiac dysrhythmia. Plays tennis regularly.

Physical Exam: Slight pectus excavatum. Cardiac auscultation normal.

Clinical Studies: Electrocardiogram (ECG): nor-mal. Echocardiogram: mild mitral valve prolapse, normal left atrial, and left ventricular (LV) size and function. No mitral regurgitation.

Diagnosis: Mitral valve prolapse.

Impairment Rating: 0% (class 0) According to Table 4-5, the objective test results, physical findings, and history all place the patient in class 0, impairment rating 0%.

CLASS 1

2% to 10% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 4-2: VALVULAR HEART DISEASE

Subject: 38-year-old woman.

History: She played collegiate sports and is cur-rently a marathon runner. She has always taken anti-biotics for dental work. NYHA class I.

Current Symptoms: Denies dyspnea, angina, palpi-tations, and fatigue.

Physical Exam: Blood pressure (BP) is normal. Pulse rate: 52 beats per minute (BPM); midpeaking systolic ejection murmur.

Clinical Studies: Echocardiogram: Bicuspid aortic valve; mean gradient of 22 mm Hg; valve area 1.6 cm2. ECG: Normal except for bradycardia. Chest radiograph: Normal.

Diagnosis: Asymptomatic mild aortic stenosis.

Impairment Rating: 6% (class 1C). According to Table 4-5, the objective test results, physical find-ings, and history all place the patient in class 1, impairment rating 6%.

CLASS 3 24% to 40% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 4-3: VALVULAR HEART DISEASE

Subject: 50-year-old man.

History: Mitral valve replacement 2 years earlier; advanced symptoms and signs of CHF causing pul-monary and systemic congestion. Activities remain limited by dyspnea on minimal exertion despite restriction of activities and salt intake. Digoxin and diuretics did not relieve symptoms. Vigorous diuretic use eliminated peripheral edema but resulted in chemical evidence of prerenal azotemia.

Current Symptoms: Walks a city block at a slow pace, drives, sleeps comfortably; breathless after climbing 1 flight of stairs.

Physical Exam: Comfortable at rest; BP 110/70 mm Hg; heart rate at 80 BPM; jugular venous pressure normal; no peripheral edema; auscultation of lungs indicates rales at the left base; apical impulse nor-mal; parasternal heave; prosthetic valve sounds are normal; I/VI holosystolic murmur at the apex.

Clinical Studies: ECG: normal sinus rhythm (NSR), heart rate of 80 BPM, low T-wave amplitude. Chest radiograph: Cardiomegaly with enlarged left ventricle, right ventricle, and left atria. Prominent pulmonary vascularity in all lung fields with no Kerley B lines. Properly positioned prosthetic valve. Echocardiogram: Enlarged ventricles and left atrium. Moderate global reduction of LV systolic function; LVEF of 35%. Well-seated prosthetic valve. Normal mean gradient across the prosthetic valve. Normal degree of regurgitation. Cardiac catheterization and angiography: LV pressure 110/18 mm Hg. Mean left atrial pressure 20 mm Hg. Pulmonary artery pressure 45/18 mm Hg. LV angiogram: mild mitral regurgitation; reduction of ventricular contraction. Level of BNP moderately elevated.

Diagnosis: Mitral valve replacement with a prosthe-sis; LV dysfunction, probable rheumatic origin.

Impairment Rating: 32% (class 3C). Refer to Table 4-5; the objective test results, physical findings, and history all place the patient in class 3C impairment rating 32%.

CLASS 4 45% to 65% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 4-4: VALVULAR HEART DISEASE

Subject: 45-year-old woman.

History: Congestive HF for 10 years; breathless-ness and fatigue with minimal exertion; diuretics, digoxin, and, for the past year, peripheral vasodilator did not relieve symptoms. Sleeps on 3 pillows. Long-term ankle edema. Protuberant abdomen for last year. Unable to do most ADLs without assistance.

Physical Exam: Pale and weak; thin; jaundiced face showed temporal depression; respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute; BP 110 /70 mm Hg; heart rate irregular at 80 BPM. Patient prefers sitting position. Neck veins distended. Prominent V waves. Lung sounds: rales at both lung bases; parasternal heave. III/VI harsh long systolic murmur in the second right intercostal space that lasts to late systole, fol-lowed by a long loud decrescendo diastolic murmur, blowing holosystolic murmur at the lower sternal border, middiastolic rumble at the apex. Diminished S1; S2 loud at the second left intercostal space. Liver was large, pulsatile, approximately 12-cm ascites. Pitting edema of thighs, sacral area, and legs.

Clinical Studies: ECG: NSR, irregular ventricular response, 80 BPM, low voltage QRS and T waves. Chest radiograph: Massive cardiomegaly. Vascular prominence and Kerley B lines on both sides of the upper lobes. Echocardiogram: Enlargement of all chambers; LVEF 20%. Two-dimensional echocar-diography identifies heavy calcification of the aortic and mitral valves. Doppler studies identify severe aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation, tricuspid regur-gitation, moderate aortic regurgitation, and mitral stenosis. Pulmonary artery pressure 70 mm Hg.

Diagnosis: Aortic and mitral stenosis and regurgita-tion, tricuspid regurgitation.

Impairment Rating: 65% (class 4E). All 3 factors are class 4; therefore, the highest rating is given.

4.3 Coronary Artery Disease

4.3a Criteria for Rating Impairment due to Coronary Artery Disease

Coronary artery disease relates specifically to dis-eases of the coronary arteries, most commonly arte-riosclerotic in nature. The degree of arteriosclerosis will vary from mild luminal irregularities causing no impairment to severely narrowed coronary arteries impairing daily activities. In addition, plaque rupture may occur, resulting in acute myocardial infarction with resultant significant LV impairment. Additional etiologies of coronary artery narrowing include vasospasm, embolic events, congenital abnormali-ties, Kawasaki disease, trauma, a connective tissue disorder such as lupus, or prior radiation therapy.

Angina pectoris results from an imbalance in myocardial oxygen demand in the presence of chron-ically reduced coronary blood flow. Medication can often control the symptoms; however, if fixed obstructive disease is severe, angina may also be present even at rest. Myocardial infarction is diag-nosed if 2 of the 3 following clinical conditions are met: acute ECG changes, elevated myocardial enzyme levels including troponin,15 or evidence of myocardial damage by imaging studies. Symptoms of chest pain are not required for myocardial infarc-tion, as at least 25% of myocardial infarctions are “silent” with no evidence of chest pain. The degree of the patient’s impairment can be evaluated based on Table 4-6.

Stress testing, preferably with cardiac imaging techniques, serves as the mainstay in evaluating the degree of damage and thus impairment due to CAD. Left ventricular function must be determined in these individuals as an objective basis for impair-ment rating. Coronary angiography is also included in the impairment classification tables, as it enables the quantitative assessment of atherosclerotic dis-ease.2,16 Newer imaging techniques, such as cardiac MRI and CT angiography, also accurately quantify atherosclerotic disease and may be used for impair-ment rating purposes.

Impairment can be markedly altered with treatment programs such as cardiac rehabilitation, smoking cessation, and compliance with medications. Patients often require intervention for their CAD that may be percutaneous (ie, percutaneous transluminal coro-nary angioplasty [PTCA] and/or stent placement), or they may require coronary artery bypass grafting. Impairment ratings should be determined after these

procedures have been completed and the patient is at MMI, generally 3 to 6 months later.

CLASS 0 0% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 4-5: CORONARY ARTERY DISEASE

Subject: 48-year-old asymptomatic woman.

History: No cardiac history; underwent treadmill stress test for an insurance physical and was found to have inferior electrical changes, with normal exercise tolerance.

Symptoms: None.

Physical Exam: Normal.

Clinical Studies: ECG: Normal.

Cardiac Catheterization: Normal coronary anatomy and no evidence of atherosclerotic coronary disease. Normal EF.

Diagnosis: No evidence of coronary disease, false-positive treadmill stress test.

Impairment Rating: 0% (class 0) (Table 4-6).

CLASS 2 11% to 23% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 4-6: CORONARY ARTERY DISEASE

Subject: 58-year-old man.

History: Referred to a cardiologist because of an abnormal myocardial perfusion scan. Denies any significant chest pain or dyspnea.

Current Symptoms: Plays golf and tennis regularly. States he has the same level of endurance he had in college. Nonsmoker. No history of hypertension, dia-betes mellitus, or family history of CAD. Concerned because his friend just died unexpectedly of a heart attack 2 months earlier. Wanted to know definitely if he had any significant CAD because he was on a short list of possible High Court nominees.

Physical Exam: Normal, including vital signs.

Clinical Studies: Exercise echocardiogram: Normal exercise tolerance (9 minutes per Bruce protocol). Peak heart rate of 180 BPM. Nine METs. No ECG changes. Mild anterior wall hypokinesis. Lab studies: Total cholesterol 9.45 mmol/L (365 mg/dL).

High-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) 1.17 mmol/L (45 mg/dL). Triglycerides 2.54 mmol/L (225 mg/dL). Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) 7.12 mmol/L (275 mg/dL). Cardiac catheterization: 50% lesions in proximal and distal LAD, right coronary artery and left circumflex. Scattered 20% and 30% luminal irregularities throughout. Ejection fraction is 65%.

Diagnosis: Asymptomatic CAD.

Impairment Rating: 11% (class 2B). According to Table 4-6, the objective test findings place the patient in class 2C, impairment rating 17%; however, both the history and physical exam are con-sistent with class 1. His functional capacity is excel-lent; therefore, the final impairment rating is 11%, the initial median of 17% adjusted to 14% based on history followed by additional adjustment to 11% according to the physical exam.

EXAMPLE 4-7: CORONARY ARTERY DISEASE

Subject: 52-year-old woman.

History: Service specialist for an insurance firm. Coronary artery bypass grafting 6 months earlier. LIMA to left anterior descending artery and RIMA to right coronary artery. Preoperative coronary angi-ography identified no significant obstructive disease in the left circumflex artery. Preoperative LV func-tion was normal. Sedentary job. Previous exertional angina.

Current symptoms: Did well after surgery and worked for 14 months. Asymptomatic. Avoids heavy physical exertion. Only medication is daily aspirin.

Physical Exam: Well-healed scar. Normal cardio-vascular exam at rest.

Clinical Studies: Bruce protocol exercise 10 days earlier to a heart rate of 160 BPM. No ST-T wave changes or dysrhythmias after 10 minutes of exer-cise. Achieved greater than 7 METs. Shows exer-tional tachycardia with delayed recovery to baseline. Concurrent metabolic study shows VO2max 18 mL/ kg/min/. Baseline ECG showed no Q waves. Chest radiograph: Normal.

Diagnosis: CAD, post–coronary artery bypass grafting.

Impairment Rating: 17% (class 2C). According to Table 4-6, the objective test findings, physical findings, and history place the patient in class 2C, impairment rating 17%.

EXAMPLE 4-8: CORONARY ARTERY DISEASE

Subject: 48-year-old man.

History: Chest pain for 2 years interrupted his work-day. Pain accompanied by diaphoresis and dyspnea. Slightly elevated cholesterol: 6.34 mmol/L (245 mg/ dL). Family history: His 66-year-old father is living with CAD.

Current Symptoms: Chest pain. Palpitations.

Physical Exam: Blood pressure 140/90 mm/Hg. Heart rate 76 BPM. Occasional ectopic beats; other-wise normal heart sounds.

Clinical Studies: Exercise stress test was completed to 14 minutes; maximum heart rate 172; no exercise-induced ischemia. Due to persistence of seeking a second opinion, he was referred to a cardiologist and underwent cardiac catheterization which showed 50% stenosis in the right coronary artery, 60% EF. He returned to work. Symptoms persisted for another 6 months. Holter monitor showed no ST-segment ele-vation during pain. A second cardiologist suspected coronary artery spasm. He received ergonovine testing documenting coronary spasm of the right coronary artery. He was placed on a calcium channel blocker and has no current symptoms.

Diagnosis: Vasospastic angina pectoris; coronary artery vasospasm induced with significant mental stress only.

Impairment Rating: 17% (class 2C). According to Table 4-6, the objective test findings place patient in class 2C. The history of no further symptoms and physical examination are both consistent with class 2.

CLASS 4 45% to 65% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 4-9: CORONARY ARTERY DISEASE

Subject: 46-year-old woman.

History: Coronary artery bypass surgery 11 months earlier; daily pain, weakness, and breathlessness after minimal exertion. Often experiences angina at rest.

Current Symptoms: Uses 3 pillows. Awakens short of breath. Commonly sleeps sitting in a chair. Symptoms continue despite treatment with digitalis, diuretics, nitrates, calcium channel blocking agents,

and an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor.

Physical Exam: Evidence of weight loss. Prefers sitting position. Blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg. Heart rate 92 BPM. Distended neck veins with abdominal hand pressure even when upper part of the exam table is at 45 degrees. Apical impulse is enlarged, sustained, and displaced. A parasternal heave is noted. Rales at both lung bases. Dullness at the right lung base. Auscultation reveals a soft S1, prominent S3, II/VI holosystolic murmur at the apex.

4.4 Cardiomyopathies

4.4a Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to Cardiomyopathies

Cardiomyopathy is a disease that affects the heart muscles. The standard means of quantifying car-diomyopathy involves measuring left systolic and diastolic function as well as right ventricular (RV) function using echocardiography. The BNP mea-surements provide additional objective evidence of classic CHF. The causes of cardiomyopathy are quite diverse7 and may include the following:

1. Systolic dysfunction secondary to myocardial infarction.

2. Diastolic dysfunction secondary to long-standing hypertension.

3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

4. Cardiomyopathy of obesity.

5. Cardiomyopathy secondary to systemic causes, such as hyperthyroidism or chronic alcohol exposure.

Cardiomyopathy may be described according to 3 basic pathophysiologic types:

1. Dilated or congestive.

2. Hypertrophic.

3. Restrictive.

Impairment should be evaluated in the context of medication use and surgical intervention. For example, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy may war-rant myectomy, resulting in complete resolution of symptoms.

Brief mention should be made of the expanded recommendations for use of automatic implantable cardiac defibrillators (AICDs).17 Most patients with significantly impaired LV function will meet crite-ria for AICD implantation, and this intervention is included in the impairment classification table (Table 4-7). Biventricular pacing is also a new tech-nology used in classes 3 and 4 patients with HF that has been shown to improve functional status.18

4.5 Pericardial Heart Disease

4.5a Criteria for Rating Impairment due to Pericardial Disease

Pericardial disease is not nearly as common as the previous entities discussed; however, it will occasionally warrant an evaluation of impairment. Inflammation of the pericardium may occur due to infection (most commonly viral), or may occur fol-lowing coronary artery bypass grafting (after peri-cardiotomy syndrome) or after myocardial infarction (Dressler’s syndrome). In addition, connective tissue disorders such as lupus, radiation-induced pericardi-tis, and tumor etiologies must be considered. There is very rarely tumor involvement in the pericardium as well. Often, the cause remains idiopathic.

Recurrent pericarditis can be quite disabling. Although echocardiography is helpful to diagnose a pericardial effusion, such effusion is not essential for the diagnosis of pericarditis. Laboratory values are helpful, most specifically an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR).

Constrictive pericarditis is an unusual entity and deserves brief discussion. True constrictive pericar-ditis often requires surgical intervention and removal of the pericardium. Constrictive pericarditis may be quite disabling and characterized by persistent symptoms of CHF.

Cardiac tamponade is a rare but life-threatening complication of pericarditis, often associated with the presence of carcinoma, or a history of chest trauma. Cardiac tamponade generally requires pericardiocentesis, which may be curative, with no resulting permanent impairment.

The physical examination findings can be variable or absent. The examiner may hear a pericardial fric-tion rub or pericardial “knock”; these findings are

pathognomonic of pericarditis. The pericardium may require more thorough evaluation such as CT or MRI to evaluate thickness of the pericardium. See Table 4-8 for impairment rating criteria.

4.6 Dysrhythmias

4.6a Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to Dysrhythmias

Cardiac dysrhythmias vary in severity from completely benign to life-threatening, and include tachydysrhyth-mias and bradydysrhythmias. Echocardiography and Holter monitoring remain a mainstay for evaluation of affected individuals. In general, cardiac dysrhyth-mias are markedly less severe when they occur in the absence of organic heart disease than in the presence of structural heart disease.

Dysrhythmias are somewhat difficult to evaluate because they vary in frequency as well as severity. Symptoms may be limited to brief palpitations or may result in life-threatening syncope. The symp-toms also may, unfortunately, be vague and limited to dyspnea, weakness, or fatigue.

Impairment evaluation for both tachydysrhythmias and bradydysrhythmias relates directly to degree of organic heart disease, and often one must use the coronary heart disease, valvular heart disease, or cardiomyopathy impairment rating tables for the most appropriate impairment determination.

The treatment of dysrhythmias has advanced signifi-cantly in the past few years. Many patients receive AICD after myocardial infarction to prevent sudden death from cardiac dysrhythmias. The presence of an AICD may specifically affect disability in certain occupations (ie, welding).

Permanent pacemakers are extremely common, particularly for bradydysrhythmias. Impairment should be evaluated post-pacemaker implantation with reassessment of symptoms.

Many dysrhythmias are controlled with medication and, in fact, may be completely stabilized, resulting in class 1 impairment estimations. See Table 4-9 for the impairment rating criteria.

4.8 Vascular Diseases Affecting the Extremities

4.8a Criteria for Rating Impairment due to Vascular Diseases of the Extemities

The presence of peripheral vascular disease is more common than previously suspected. Peripheral vas-cular disease that contributes to permanent impair-ment may include the following:

1. Atherosclerosis of the arterial system may result in intermittent claudication, atrophic changes, ulceration, gangrene, and ultimately extremity loss. Raynaud’s phenomenon must also be con-sidered when evaluating arterial disorders of the extremities.

2. Venous disorders such as chronic deep vein throm-boses resulting in pain, edema and ulceration.

3. Lymphatic disorders often leading to chronic lymphedema and recurrent infections.

Atherosclerosis remains the number one cause of arterial disorders. Raynaud’s phenomenon and thromboangiitis obliterans must also be considered when evaluating arterial disorders. Varicose veins and deep venous thromboses must be evaluated when considering the venous system. The lymphatic system is most commonly impaired by an infectious or neoplastic process.

Impairment secondary to diseases of the extremities has been divided into lower and upper extremities with two separate impairment classification tables.

In evaluating occlusive peripheral arterial disease of the lower extremity, ankle-brachial indices are an excel-lent non-invasive standard measurement. ABI values are mildly to moderately diminished between 0.41 and 0.90, severely decreased when less than or equal to 0.40. These values have been validated to have prog-nostic value.20 If the ABI’s are not felt reliable second-ary to advanced age or diabetes, the toe-brachial index should be considered.20 Duplex ultrasound can estab-lish the diagnosis of lower extremity peripheral arterial disease and establishing severity.20

4.9 Diseases of the Pulmonary Artery

4.9a Criteria for Rating Impairment due to Diseases of the Pulmonary Artery

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progres-sive and debilitating disease whose true etiology often remains unknown. Causes of PAH include pulmo-nary venous and capillary disorders, HF, pulmonary emboli, pulmonary parenchymal disease, and obesity. Mitral Valve Disease can affect the presence of PAH and must be considered in evaluating this impairment.

Classic findings of pulmonary hypertension on physi-cal examination include RV lift and an increased S2 pulmonary component on auscultation. Pulmonary

hypertension is typically diagnosed on echocardiogra-phy by estimated Doppler flow measurements across the tricuspid valve,5 often with associated echocar-diographic evidence of RV hypertrophy. Pulmonary hypertension may also be suspected from ECG changes. A right heart catheterization is rarely neces-sary to make the diagnosis of pulmonary hypertension due to the accuracy of Doppler echocardiography.13
